title: 22. Interview: PostgreSQL
summary: Interview Q&A for PostgreSQL — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 PostgreSQL interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. How does MVCC work, and what are its trade-offs?
**Answer:** PostgreSQL's MVCC keeps multiple versions of each row. When a transaction updates row R, instead of overwriting R in place, PostgreSQL creates a new version R' and leaves R intact. Concurrent readers continue to see R (the version valid when their transaction started); the writer doesn't block them. After the writer commits, new transactions see R'. The old R becomes a "dead tuple" — not deleted immediately, but marked reclaimable. **Autovacuum** periodically scans tables and removes dead tuples, freeing space. Trade-offs: (1) **Bloat** — heavy update workloads create many dead tuples; if autovacuum can't keep up, the table and indexes bloat, slowing seq scans and increasing memory pressure. (2) **Transaction ID wraparound** — every row version has an `xmin`/`xmax` (transaction ID); PostgreSQL has only 2^32 XIDs, so old XIDs must be "frozen" (replaced with a special marker) before they wrap around and cause data loss. Autovacuum handles this, but a misconfigured autovacuum has caused famous outages (Salesforce 2013). (3) **No in-place updates** — every UPDATE is effectively INSERT + DELETE, more WAL, more I/O. (4) **Long-running transactions block vacuum** — vacuum can't reclaim dead tuples that are still visible to an open transaction; a single stuck transaction can bloat the entire database. Real-world: PostgreSQL's MVCC is purer than MySQL InnoDB's (which uses undo logs in a rollback segment); the trade-off is more bloat but simpler crash recovery.
**Visual:**
```
MVCC version chain for row id=42:

  T=10: INSERT id=42, balance=1000  -> version v1 (xmin=10, xmax=0)
  T=20: UPDATE balance=900          -> v1 (xmax=20), v2 (xmin=20, xmax=0)
  T=30: UPDATE balance=850          -> v2 (xmax=30), v3 (xmin=30, xmax=0)

  Reader at snapshot 25 sees v2 (balance=900)
  Reader at snapshot 35 sees v3 (balance=850)

  Vacuum at T=40 reclaims v1 and v2 (dead tuples)

Trade-off: writers don't block readers, but table bloats
           until vacuumed; long-running txn blocks vacuum
```

### Q2. What is the WAL and why is it critical?
**Answer:** The Write-Ahead Log is an append-only sequence of records describing every change to the database. Before PostgreSQL modifies a data page, it writes the change to the WAL and fsyncs the WAL file — the change is durable at this point, even though the data page is still only in memory. The data page is flushed to disk later by the background writer in batches (random I/O, amortized). On crash, PostgreSQL replays the WAL from the last checkpoint forward, redoing every committed change — bringing the database back to a consistent state. Benefits: (1) **Durability with low latency** — fsync a single append-only file (sequential I/O, ~1 ms) instead of fsyncing every modified data page (random I/O, ~10 ms each). (2) **Crash recovery** — replay the WAL to restore consistency; uncommitted transactions are rolled back. (3) **Replication substrate** — standbys receive the WAL stream over TCP and apply it locally; this is the basis for streaming replication. (4) **Point-in-time recovery** — keep WAL archives (e.g., in S3) and replay them up to a chosen timestamp to recover from a `DROP TABLE` disaster. Trade-offs: (1) **WAL bandwidth** — heavy write workloads saturate WAL write bandwidth; throughput is capped. (2) **WAL archive storage** — keeping days of WAL archives for PITR consumes GBs. (3) **fsync latency** — every commit pays the fsync cost; `synchronous_commit=off` trades durability for throughput (lose last few commits on crash). Real-world: Netflix's Aurora PostgreSQL pushes WAL to a distributed storage layer that 6-way replicates across AZs.
**Visual:**
```
WAL crash recovery sequence:

  T=0  BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal=900 WHERE id=42;
  T=1  -> WAL append: [XID=100, UPDATE accounts id=42 bal=900]
  T=2  -> fsync WAL file   (DURABLE NOW, even if data page not flushed)
  T=3  -> modify data page in shared_buffers (still in RAM)
  T=4  COMMIT;
  T=5  -> WAL append: [XID=100 COMMIT]; fsync
  T=6  -> ack client "committed"

  T=7  CRASH (data page still in RAM, not on disk)

  Restart:
  T=8  -> Read WAL from last checkpoint
  T=9  -> REDO: apply [UPDATE accounts id=42 bal=900]
  T=10 -> REDO: apply [XID=100 COMMIT]
  T=11 -> Database consistent: balance=900
```

### Q3. How does streaming replication work, and what's the difference between sync and async?
**Answer:** Streaming replication: a standby connects to the primary over TCP and requests WAL records. The primary sends each WAL record as it's generated; the standby applies it locally, maintaining an identical copy. The standby is read-only (in hot standby mode). **Asynchronous** replication: the primary commits locally and returns to the client immediately; the standby catches up later. Trade-off: low commit latency on the primary, but if the primary fails before the standby catches up, the last few transactions are lost (data-loss window = replication lag, typically milliseconds to seconds). **Synchronous** replication (`synchronous_standby_names`): the primary waits for the standby to ack that it received (and optionally applied) the WAL record before returning COMMIT to the client. Trade-off: zero data loss, but commit latency = round-trip to standby (1–5 ms LAN, 50–100 ms cross-region). PostgreSQL offers multiple sync levels: `REMOTE_WRITE` (standby has written to OS, not fsynced — fast, small loss window on dual failure), `REMOTE_FLUSH` (fsynced — durable), `REMOTE_APPLY` (applied to data — standby reads see it). Real-world: Netflix's billing uses synchronous replication to a same-AZ standby (zero data loss for money), with async replication to a cross-region standby (DR only). Most apps use async — the latency penalty of sync isn't worth it.
**Visual:**
```
Streaming replication timeline:

  Primary                  Standby (sync)         Standby (async)
  -------                  --------------         ---------------
  BEGIN UPDATE id=42       
  WAL: [upd id=42]
  fsync WAL                recv [upd id=42]       recv [upd id=42]
  -> send to standbys      
  COMMIT                   recv [commit]          recv [commit]
  WAL: [commit]
  fsync WAL                
  wait for sync ack...     apply + ack "applied"  (catching up...)
  -> ack client "committed"
  
  Latency: +5ms (sync RTT)   Latency: 0ms (no wait)
  Loss:    0 (sync acked)    Loss:   up to lag (~50ms)

Netflix billing: sync to same-AZ standby (0 data loss for money)
                 async to cross-region (DR only)
```

### Q4. When should you use JSONB vs a fully-normalized schema?
**Answer:** Use **JSONB** when: (1) The schema varies per row — user preferences (some users have 5 fields, others have 50), event payloads (different event types have different fields), A/B test variants. (2) The fields are read as a unit ("show me the user's full profile") rather than individually queried. (3) The fields are mostly write-once-read-many and rarely updated individually. (4) The data is semi-structured (parsed from external JSON APIs). Use **normalized columns** when: (1) The field is queried individually and frequently (`WHERE email = ?`). (2) The field needs strong constraints (foreign key, unique, not null). (3) The field is updated frequently (updating a JSONB field rewrites the whole JSONB value). (4) The field needs a type beyond JSON (numeric range, timestamp with timezone, enum). Best practice: hybrid — keep stable, queryable fields as columns (user_id, email, created_at); keep variable, document-like fields as JSONB (preferences, metadata). Index JSONB with a GIN index for fast `@>` (contains) queries, or extract hot fields as **generated columns** (`ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN city TEXT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (metadata->>'address'->>'city') STORED`) and index those — gives you JSONB flexibility with column-level query performance. Real-world: Instagram stores post metadata as JSONB (varies by content type) but keeps `user_id`, `created_at`, `post_id` as columns for indexing.
**Visual:**
```
Hybrid schema (best of both):

  CREATE TABLE users (
    user_id    BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,           -- relational, indexed
    email      TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,         -- relational, unique idx
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),    -- relational
    metadata   JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'   -- document, GIN-indexed
  );
  CREATE INDEX idx_users_meta_gin ON users USING GIN (metadata);

  -- query fixed fields (columnar, B-tree, fast):
  SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'alice@x.com';

  -- query JSONB fields (GIN, fast):
  SELECT * FROM users WHERE metadata @> '{"role":"admin"}';
  SELECT * FROM users WHERE metadata->'address'->>'city' = 'NYC';

  -- extract hot JSONB field as generated column:
  ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN city TEXT
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS (metadata->'address'->>'city') STORED;
  CREATE INDEX idx_users_city ON users(city);

When to use what:
  + JSONB: schema varies, read as unit, write-once, semi-structured
  + Column: queried individually, constrained, frequently updated, typed
```

### Q5. What are PostgreSQL extensions and why are they important?
**Answer:** PostgreSQL extensions are dynamically-loaded modules that add types, functions, operators, index methods, and even custom scan providers to a running PostgreSQL backend — without forking the codebase or restarting the server. `CREATE EXTENSION pgvector;` installs vector types (`vector`), similarity operators (`<->`), and index methods (HNSW, IVFFlat) — turning PostgreSQL into a vector database for RAG applications. This is a huge deal: instead of running a separate vector DB (Pinecone, Weaviate), you get vector search on your existing relational data, in the same transaction, with the same backup/replication infrastructure. Other key extensions: **PostGIS** (geospatial — used by Uber, Foursquare, Mapbox for routing and search-by-radius), **TimescaleDB** (hypertables for time-series — IoT, monitoring), **Citus** (distributed sharding for write-scale), **pg_partman** (automated partition management), **pg_stat_statements** (query performance tracking), **pg_cron** (scheduled jobs inside PostgreSQL), **postgres_fdw** (federated queries to other PostgreSQL instances), **pglogical** (advanced logical replication). Trade-offs: (1) Cloud providers limit which extensions are allowed (RDS supports ~80; Aurora ~70; self-hosted = all). (2) Extensions can break across major version upgrades — test before upgrading. (3) Extensions run in the backend process — a buggy extension can crash PostgreSQL. Real-world: pgvector adoption in 2023-24 was explosive — every major PostgreSQL cloud now ships it, and many teams replaced their standalone vector DB with pgvector.
**Visual:**
```
PostgreSQL core + extension model:

  +----------------------------------+
  |        PostgreSQL core           |
  |  (planner, executor, WAL, MVCC, |
  |   replication, SQL parser)       |
  +----------------------------------+
       ^    ^    ^    ^    ^    ^
       |    |    |    |    |    |
  +----++--+--+--+--+--+--+--+---+
  |pgvec|PostG|Times|Citus|pg_p | ...  (extensions, loaded via
  |tor  |IS   |cale |     |artm |      CREATE EXTENSION)
  +-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+

  Each extension reuses the core's planner, executor, WAL, replication
  -> no new infrastructure to operate
  -> same backup/restore/HA story

  Top extensions:
    pgvector     - vector similarity (LLM/RAG)
    PostGIS      - geospatial (Uber, Foursquare)
    TimescaleDB  - time-series (IoT, monitoring)
    Citus        - distributed sharding
    pg_partman   - partition automation
    pg_stat_statements - query perf
    postgres_fdw - federated queries
```

### Q6. How does declarative partitioning work, and what are its limitations?
**Answer:** Declarative partitioning (PostgreSQL 10+) splits a table into partitions by **RANGE** (e.g., date), **LIST** (e.g., region), or **HASH** (e.g., user_id). The parent table is a virtual "container"; data lives in child partitions. Queries that filter by the partition key use **partition pruning** — the planner examines the WHERE clause and skips partitions that can't possibly contain matching rows, turning a 10 TB table scan into a 100 GB scan. Benefits: (1) **Drop old data fast** — `DROP TABLE events_2023_01` is instant, vs `DELETE FROM events WHERE dt < '2023-02-01'` which bloats the table. (2) **Smaller indexes per partition** — each partition has its own indexes, faster to scan and maintain. (3) **Parallel maintenance** — vacuum and reindex run per-partition, in parallel. (4) **Tiered storage** — old partitions on cheap HDD, current on NVMe. Limitations: (1) **No global unique constraints** — you can't enforce `UNIQUE(email)` across partitions unless `email` is in the partition key. (2) **Foreign keys** — PostgreSQL 12+ allows FKs to partitioned tables, but performance is worse than non-partitioned. (3) **Row movement on update** — if an UPDATE changes the partition key, PostgreSQL moves the row (DELETE + INSERT), which is expensive. (4) **Planner mistakes** — occasionally fails to prune partitions if the WHERE clause uses a function on the partition key. Real-world: Netflix partitions billing events by month; old months are archived to S3 via `pg_dump` + `DROP TABLE`.
**Visual:**
```
Range partitioning by month:

  events (parent, virtual)
  +-- events_2023_01  (dt in [2023-01, 2023-02))  -- archived
  +-- events_2023_02  (dt in [2023-02, 2023-03))  -- archived
  +-- events_2023_03  (dt in [2023-03, 2023-04))  -- archived
  +-- events_2023_04  (dt in [2023-04, 2023-05))  -- current

  Query: SELECT * FROM events WHERE dt = '2023-04-15';
  Planner prunes to events_2023_04 only (1/4 partitions scanned)

  Drop old data: DROP TABLE events_2023_01;  (instant, no bloat)
  vs DELETE FROM events WHERE dt < '2023-02'; (bloats, slow)

Limitations:
  + UNIQUE(email) across all partitions NOT possible
    (unless email is in partition key)
  + UPDATE changing dt = moves row (expensive)
  + FK to partitioned table: supported in PG12+ but slower
```

### Q7. What is autovacuum and how do you tune it?
**Answer:** Autovacuum is PostgreSQL's background process that reclaims dead tuples (old row versions left by MVCC updates and deletes) and freezes old transaction IDs (to prevent XID wraparound). Without autovacuum, dead tuples accumulate, tables and indexes bloat, seq scans slow down, and eventually XID wraparound forces PostgreSQL into single-user "protective" mode (a famous outage cause). Autovacuum runs continuously, launching workers per database based on: `autovacuum_vacuum_threshold` (default 50 dead tuples) + `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` (default 0.2, so a table with 1M rows triggers vacuum at 50 + 0.2*1M = 200k dead tuples). It also runs `ANALYZE` (statistics update) on similar thresholds. Tuning: (1) **Lower `scale_factor` for high-update tables** — `ALTER TABLE events SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.05)` triggers vacuum more often, keeping bloat low. (2) **Increase `autovacuum_max_workers`** (default 3) for databases with many tables. (3) **Increase `autovacuum_naptime`** (default 1 min) for less aggressive vacuum on quiet tables. (4) **Tune cost limits** — autovacuum throttles itself to avoid impacting query performance; `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` (default 200) controls how much I/O it does before sleeping. (5) **Watch for "autovacuum stuck"** — a long-running transaction blocks vacuum on the rows it sees; kill the long-running txn. (6) **Monitor bloat** — `pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup` tells you when a table needs vacuum. Real-world: Salesforce's 2013 outage was XID wraparound due to autovacuum disabled; they re-enabled it and now monitor `n_dead_tup` and XID age aggressively.
**Visual:**
```
Autovacuum triggers and tuning:

  Per-table trigger:
    vacuum when: dead_tuples > 50 + (0.2 * total_rows)
    Example: 1M-row table -> vacuum at 200k dead tuples

  Tuning knobs:
    autovacuum_max_workers = 3 (raise for many tables)
    autovacuum_naptime = 1min (lower for faster reaction)
    autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = 200 (raise for faster vacuum,
                                        more I/O impact on queries)

  Per-table overrides (high-update tables):
    ALTER TABLE events SET (
      autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.05,  -- vacuum at 5% dead
      autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.02  -- analyze at 2% changed
    );

  Monitor:
    SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, n_live_tup,
           last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze
    FROM pg_stat_user_tables;

  Failure modes:
    + long-running txn -> blocks vacuum on visible rows
    + autovacuum off -> XID wraparound -> protective single-user mode
      (Salesforce 2013 outage)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Instagram wants to store posts where each post type (photo, video, carousel, reel) has different metadata. Design the schema on PostgreSQL.
**Answer:** Use a hybrid schema with stable columns + JSONB metadata. Stable fields (queried frequently, indexed): `post_id BIGINT PK`, `user_id BIGINT` (indexed for "all posts by user X"), `created_at TIMESTAMPTZ` (indexed for "recent posts"), `post_type TEXT` (enum: photo/video/carousel/reel), `caption TEXT`. Variable fields in `metadata JSONB`: photo has `{width, height, s3_key, exif}`; video has `{duration, codec, s3_key, thumbnail_key}`; carousel has `{items: [{s3_key, width, height}, ...]}`; reel has `{duration, audio_track_id, s3_key}`. Add a GIN index on `metadata` for queries like "find all reels with audio_track_id=X". For hot JSONB paths, add generated columns: `ALTER TABLE posts ADD COLUMN duration INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS ((metadata->>'duration')::int) STORED` and a B-tree index — gives column-level query performance on a JSONB field. Partition by `created_at` (range, monthly) so old posts can be archived. Partition by `user_id` hash if a single user's posts don't fit one shard. Real-world: Instagram actually uses a custom PostgreSQL fork with application-layer sharding by user_id; the schema pattern above matches what they've described in engineering talks. Trade-off: JSONB fields can't be foreign-keyed (a reel's `audio_track_id` can't FK to an `audio_tracks` table); enforce referential integrity in app code or use triggers.
**Visual:**
```
Instagram posts on PostgreSQL (hybrid schema):

  CREATE TABLE posts (
    post_id    BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    post_type  TEXT NOT NULL,  -- photo|video|carousel|reel
    caption    TEXT,
    metadata   JSONB NOT NULL
  );
  CREATE INDEX idx_posts_user_time ON posts(user_id, created_at DESC);
  CREATE INDEX idx_posts_meta_gin  ON posts USING GIN (metadata);

  -- generated column for hot JSONB field:
  ALTER TABLE posts ADD COLUMN duration INT
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS ((metadata->>'duration')::int) STORED;
  CREATE INDEX idx_posts_duration ON posts(duration);

  -- partition by month:
  CREATE TABLE posts PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
  CREATE TABLE posts_2024_01 PARTITION OF posts
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-02-01');
  -- ...

  Example metadata:
    photo:   {"width":1080,"height":1080,"s3_key":"p/123.jpg"}
    reel:    {"duration":15,"audio_track_id":42,"s3_key":"r/456.mp4"}
    carousel:{"items":[{"s3_key":"c/1.jpg","width":1080}, ...]}
```

### Q2. Netflix's billing service uses PostgreSQL on Aurora. A `VACUUM FULL` was run on the 2 TB `transactions` table; the database was unresponsive for 6 hours. What happened and how do you prevent it?
**Answer:** `VACUUM FULL` rewrites the entire table from scratch to reclaim space — it takes an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, blocking all reads and writes for the entire duration. On a 2 TB table, this is hours of downtime. Why was it run? Likely the table had bloated to 4 TB (50 % dead tuples) due to autovacuum not keeping up, and someone ran `VACUUM FULL` to reclaim space — not realizing it locks the table. Prevention: (1) **Never run `VACUUM FULL` on a production table during business hours** — it's an offline operation. (2) **Use `pg_repack` or `pg_squeeze`** instead — they rebuild the table online by creating a copy with triggers capturing concurrent changes, then swapping. No exclusive lock. (3) **Tune autovacuum** so the table never bloats enough to need `VACUUM FULL` in the first place — lower `scale_factor` for high-churn tables, increase `cost_limit`. (4) **Monitor bloat** — alert when `n_dead_tup / n_live_tup > 0.2`; investigate before it gets worse. (5) **For Aurora specifically** — Aurora's storage layer doesn't benefit from `VACUUM FULL` the same way (storage is already distributed); use `pg_repack` for online compaction. Real-world: Netflix's billing team replaced `VACUUM FULL` with `pg_repack` scheduled during low-traffic windows; bloat dropped from 50 % to <10 % with zero downtime.
**Visual:**
```
VACUUM FULL vs pg_repack:

  VACUUM FULL transactions:
    1. ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock (blocks reads + writes)
    2. Rewrite entire 2TB table to new file
    3. Replace old file with new
    4. 6 hours of downtime  <-- BAD

  pg_repack transactions:
    1. CREATE TABLE transactions_repack (LIKE transactions)
    2. CREATE TRIGGER log_changes (capture concurrent INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE)
    3. COPY rows to transactions_repack (in parallel)
    4. Apply logged changes to transactions_repack
    5. Rename transactions -> transactions_old,
       transactions_repack -> transactions  (sub-second lock)
    6. Drop transactions_old
    -> Zero downtime, same bloat reduction

  Prevent bloat in the first place:
    + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.05 (per-table)
    + monitor n_dead_tup, alert at 20%
    + pg_repack weekly during low-traffic window
```

### Q3. You're migrating a 5 TB PostgreSQL database to a new major version (PG 13 to PG 15). How do you do it with minimal downtime?
**Answer:** Major version upgrades require a binary upgrade (data files aren't compatible across major versions). Options, in order of increasing complexity but decreasing downtime: (1) **`pg_upgrade --link`** (in-place, ~minutes of downtime) — runs `pg_upgrade` with `--link` mode, which hard-links data files instead of copying them, dropping downtime from hours to minutes. Requires both versions installed on the same host. Trade-off: the old cluster must be stopped during the upgrade. (2) **Logical replication** (near-zero downtime) — set up PG 15 as a logical replica of PG 13 (using `pglogical` or native logical replication in PG 14+); let it catch up; at cutover, stop writes to PG 13, let PG 15 drain, repoint app to PG 15. Downtime: seconds to minutes. Trade-off: logical replication has limitations (no DDL, no sequences unless handled separately, large tables take time to copy initially). (3) **Dump/restore** (hours of downtime) — `pg_dump` from old, `pg_restore` to new. Simple but slow; only viable for small databases or maintenance windows. For a 5 TB database, the answer is **logical replication**: (a) Provision PG 15 cluster. (b) Create publications on PG 13 (`CREATE PUBLICATION all_tables FOR ALL TABLES`). (c) Create subscriptions on PG 15 (`CREATE SUBSCRIPTION ... CONNECTION '...' PUBLICATION all_tables`). (d) PG 15 copies initial snapshot (takes hours/days for 5 TB), then streams changes. (e) Monitor lag until caught up. (f) Cutover: stop app, wait for final acks, run sequence sync, repoint app. Total downtime: under 5 minutes. Real-world: Netflix, Uber, and most large PG users use logical replication for major upgrades; Coursera documented a 0-downtime upgrade this way.
**Visual:**
```
PG 13 -> PG 15 migration (logical replication, near-zero downtime):

  Phase 1: setup (no downtime)
    PG 13 (primary, live) --logical replication--> PG 15 (new, catching up)
    - CREATE PUBLICATION on PG 13
    - CREATE SUBSCRIPTION on PG 15
    - PG 15 copies initial 5TB snapshot (hours/days)

  Phase 2: catch up (monitor lag)
    - pg_stat_subscription: lag -> 0
    - sequences synced (pglogical handles this)

  Phase 3: cutover (seconds of downtime)
    T=0  stop app (no new writes)
    T=5s wait for PG 15 to ack final LSN
    T=10s sync sequences (SELECT setval ...)
    T=15s repoint app connection string to PG 15
    T=20s start app -> reads+writes to PG 15
    T=30s verify traffic, alerting

  Total downtime: ~20-30 seconds
  Rollback plan: keep PG 13 read-only for 24h in case of bug
```

### Q4. Your PostgreSQL primary is at 90 % CPU; queries that used to take 10 ms now take 500 ms. How do you diagnose?
**Answer:** Sudden CPU spike + slow queries suggests either a query plan regression (planner picked a bad plan) or lock contention. Diagnosis steps: (1) **Check `pg_stat_activity`** — `SELECT query, state, wait_event_type, query_start FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state='active'`. Are there many queries blocked on a lock (`wait_event_type='Lock'`)? Is one query running for minutes? (2) **Check `pg_stat_statements`** — `SELECT query, calls, total_exec_time, mean_exec_time FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10`. Which queries are eating CPU? Has `mean_exec_time` spiked vs the baseline? (3) **`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`** the slow queries — did the plan change from index scan to seq scan? Likely cause: stale statistics (autovacuum/analyze hasn't run recently, or a large data load skewed the distribution). (4) **Check for autovacuum running** — a long autovacuum on a large table can hog I/O; check `pg_stat_progress_vacuum`. (5) **Check for missing indexes** — a new query pattern (e.g., a new feature querying by a column that has no index) triggers seq scans. (6) **Check connections** — `SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity`; if it's near `max_connections`, the server is thrashing between backends (connection pool issue — see Topic 16). (7) **Check for cache miss** — `SELECT sum(blks_hit)/sum(blks_hit+blks_read) FROM pg_stat_database`; if cache hit ratio dropped from 99 % to 80 %, the working set no longer fits in `shared_buffers` (data grew, or a query scans too much). Fixes: run `ANALYZE` on affected tables to refresh stats; add missing indexes; kill long-running queries; tune autovacuum to be more aggressive; increase `shared_buffers` or move to a bigger instance; use PgBouncer to reduce backend count. Real-world: most "PostgreSQL is slow" tickets are solved by `ANALYZE` (stale stats) or a missing index.
**Visual:**
```
PostgreSQL slow-query diagnosis flow:

  1. pg_stat_activity -> what's running? what's blocked?
     - many in 'active' state with wait_event_type='Lock'?
       -> lock contention (find blocker, kill if needed)
     - one query running for >5min?
       -> long-running query (kill, add statement_timeout)

  2. pg_stat_statements -> which queries eating CPU?
     - total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10
     - mean_exec_time spiked vs baseline?

  3. EXPLAIN ANALYZE slow query -> plan regression?
     - was Index Scan, now Seq Scan? -> stats stale, run ANALYZE
     - was fast, now Nested Loop with huge inner? -> stats skewed

  4. Check autovacuum: pg_stat_progress_vacuum
     - long vacuum on big table -> hogging I/O

  5. Check cache: pg_stat_database
     - blks_hit/(blks_hit+blks_read) < 90%? -> working set > shared_buffers

  6. Check connections: count in pg_stat_activity
     - near max_connections? -> thrashing, use PgBouncer

  Fixes (priority order):
    + ANALYZE affected tables (free, fast)
    + add missing index
    + kill long-running queries, set statement_timeout
    + tune autovacuum for high-churn tables
    + PgBouncer for connection multiplexing
    + bigger instance (shared_buffers, RAM) as last resort
```

### Q5. Your startup is building a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) app. Should you use pgvector on PostgreSQL or a dedicated vector DB like Pinecone?
**Answer:** Start with **pgvector on PostgreSQL**; move to a dedicated vector DB only if you outgrow it. Reasons: (1) **Operational simplicity** — your existing PostgreSQL (with backups, replication, monitoring, on-call runbooks) handles the vector workload too. No new system to operate. (2) **Transactional consistency** — embeddings are stored in the same transaction as the source text; no distributed consistency issues. (3) **Hybrid queries** — `SELECT * FROM docs JOIN embeddings USING (doc_id) WHERE docs.user_id = ? ORDER BY embeddings.embedding <-> '[...]' LIMIT 10` combines relational filter with vector similarity in one query. A dedicated vector DB would force a two-step (vector search → fetch metadata). (4) **Cost** — pgvector is free; Pinecone charges per query and per GB. Trade-offs / when to switch: (1) **Scale** — pgvector HNSW index handles ~1M vectors well, ~10M with tuning, but starts to slow at 100M+; Pinecone/Weaviate are designed for billions. (2) **Index build time** — building HNSW on 10M vectors takes hours and blocks writes; Pinecone handles this natively. (3) **Specialized algorithms** — Pinecone and Weaviate have proprietary quantization (FAISS IVF/PQ) that pgvector lacks. (4) **Multi-tenant isolation** — Pinecone has namespaces; pgvector relies on row-level security. The decision: < 10M vectors, single-tenant or simple multi-tenant → pgvector. > 100M vectors, or aggressive latency SLA, or specialized quantization needed → dedicated DB. Real-world: many startups (ChatGPT plugins, document Q&A tools) use pgvector successfully at 1-10M scale; OpenAI's docs even recommend pgvector for getting started.
**Visual:**
```
pgvector vs Pinecone/Weaviate decision:

  pgvector on PostgreSQL:
    + operational simplicity (reuse existing PG infra)
    + transactional consistency (embeddings + text in same txn)
    + hybrid queries (relational filter + vector search in one SQL)
    + free
    - limited to ~10M vectors with good perf (HNSW index)
    - index rebuild blocks writes (hours for 10M)
    - no proprietary quantization (IVF/PQ)

  Pinecone / Weaviate:
    + scales to billions of vectors
    + native index rebuild (no write blocking)
    + quantization (smaller footprint, faster search)
    + multi-tenant namespaces
    - new system to operate
    - hybrid queries need 2 steps (vector search -> fetch metadata)
    - $$ per query + per GB

  Decision:
    <10M vectors, single-tenant -> pgvector (start here)
    10-100M vectors, aggressive SLA -> benchmark both
    >100M vectors or specialized quantization -> dedicated DB
```

### Q6. You need point-in-time recovery (PITR) for compliance: restore the database to exactly 2024-03-15 14:30:00. How does PostgreSQL PITR work?
**Answer:** PITR combines a base backup with continuous WAL archiving. Setup: (1) **Enable WAL archiving** — `archive_mode = on`, `archive_command = 'aws s3 cp %p s3://my-wal-bucket/%f'`. Every WAL segment (16 MB by default) is uploaded to S3 as it fills. (2) **Take a base backup** — `pg_basebackup -D /backup/base` creates a consistent snapshot of the data files; this is your starting point. Run base backups periodically (daily is common). Restore procedure: (1) **Provision a new PostgreSQL instance** with the same major version. (2) **Copy the base backup** to the data directory. (3) **Create `recovery.signal`** in the data directory (PG 12+; replaces `recovery.conf`). (4) **Configure recovery** in `postgresql.conf`: `restore_command = 'aws s3 cp s3://my-wal-bucket/%f %p'` (fetch WAL from S3), `recovery_target_time = '2024-03-15 14:30:00+00'`. (5) **Start PostgreSQL** — it enters recovery mode, replays WAL from the base backup forward, stopping at the target timestamp. (6) **Promote** — once recovery completes, `SELECT pg_promote()` makes it a read-write primary. Trade-offs: (1) **Recovery time** — replaying days of WAL takes time; for faster PITR, take more frequent base backups (every few hours). (2) **Storage cost** — archiving every WAL segment to S3 is cheap but adds up over months; set lifecycle rules to delete old WALs. (3) **Granularity** — recovery_target_time has second-granularity; for finer control use `recovery_target_xid` or `recovery_target_lsn`. (4) **Named restore points** — `SELECT pg_create_restore_point('before_migration')` lets you recover to a specific named point (useful before risky migrations). Real-world: AWS RDS automates this — set retention period (1-35 days), restore to any second with a click.
**Visual:**
```
PostgreSQL PITR architecture:

  Production:
    base backup (daily): pg_basebackup -> S3://backups/base_2024-03-15
    WAL archive (continuous):
      pg_wal/0000000100000001.s3 -> S3://wal-bucket/0000000100000001
      pg_wal/0000000100000002.s3 -> S3://wal-bucket/0000000100000002
      ...

  Restore to 2024-03-15 14:30:00:
    1. Provision new PG instance (same major version)
    2. Copy base backup to data dir
    3. Create recovery.signal file
    4. postgresql.conf:
         restore_command = 'aws s3 cp s3://wal-bucket/%f %p'
         recovery_target_time = '2024-03-15 14:30:00+00'
    5. Start PG -> recovery mode:
       - replay WAL from base backup forward
       - stop at 2024-03-15 14:30:00
       - undo any uncommitted txns at that point
    6. SELECT pg_promote() -> read-write primary

  Recovery time: minutes (small) to hours (large, lots of WAL to replay)
  RPO (recovery point objective): 0 to a few seconds (last archived WAL)
```

### Q7. Your team is choosing between PostgreSQL and MySQL for a new OLTP service. How do you decide?
**Answer:** Both are excellent OLTP databases; the choice depends on specific needs. **Choose PostgreSQL if:** (1) You need JSONB with indexing (MongoDB-like flexibility inside a relational DB). (2) You need extensions (pgvector for AI, PostGIS for geo, TimescaleDB for time-series). (3) You need stricter SQL compliance (window functions, CTEs with recursive, full ANSI SQL). (4) You need advanced data types (arrays, ranges, custom types). (5) You need richer query plans (PostgreSQL's planner is generally smarter, especially for complex joins). (6) You value correctness over speed (PostgreSQL's MVCC is purer; constraint enforcement is stricter). **Choose MySQL if:** (1) You need maximum raw throughput on simple queries (MySQL's optimizer is faster for point lookups). (2) Your team already knows MySQL (operational familiarity matters). (3) You need a smaller footprint (MySQL uses less memory per connection — thread vs process). (4) You're on a stack that defaults to MySQL (LAMP, WordPress). (5) You need simpler replication (MySQL's binlog-based replication is conceptually simpler than PostgreSQL's WAL streaming). For modern applications, PostgreSQL has the edge — JSONB, extensions, and SQL compliance are increasingly important, and PostgreSQL's performance has caught up to MySQL on most workloads. The DB-Engines ranking reflects this: PostgreSQL is gaining, MySQL is flat. Real-world: Instagram and Netflix use both (PostgreSQL for some services, MySQL for others); the choice is per-service based on needs. For a brand-new service in 2024 with no legacy constraints, default to PostgreSQL unless you have a specific reason for MySQL.
**Visual:**
```
PostgreSQL vs MySQL decision matrix:

  Criterion               | PostgreSQL | MySQL
  ------------------------|------------|-------
  JSONB + GIN index       | ******     | **
  Extensions (pgvector..) | ******     | *
  SQL compliance (ANSI)   | ******     | ****
  Point lookup throughput | ****       | ******
  Memory per connection   | *** (10MB) | ***** (~1MB)
  Replication simplicity  | ****       | *****
  Geospatial (PostGIS)    | ******     | ***
  Team familiarity        | varies     | varies
  Cloud support (RDS)     | ******     | ******

  Default in 2024 for new service: PostgreSQL
  Reasons:
    + JSONB is killer feature for modern apps
    + pgvector for AI/RAG workloads
    + extensions add capability without new infra
    + stricter correctness, smarter planner
    + performance gap with MySQL has closed

  Pick MySQL when:
    + team knows MySQL deeply
    + simple point-lookup workload (extreme QPS)
    + legacy stack (LAMP, WordPress)
    + memory-constrained (many connections)
```

Autovacuum is PostgreSQL's background process that reclaims dead tuples (old row versions left by MVCC updates and deletes) and freezes old transaction IDs (to prevent XID wraparound).

The data page is flushed to disk later by the background writer in batches (random I/O, amortized).
